title: Whatever you ask
hookLine: whatever you ask of your own Master, He gives (Dhanasri M5, ang 681)
tomorrow: As the Word comes to me, Lalo

cards: A kid with a request runs the numbers fast: one parent for the late curfew, the other for the money, a grandparent for the extra dessert. Asking is a skill. You learn who will say yes, how to phrase it, when to wait.
Then, in Raag Dhanasri, comes a line from Guru Arjan that seems to skip all that strategy: whatever you ask of your own Master, He gives. No angles. No timing.
It sounds almost too simple. So what is it saying?

teach.b: The line is on ang 681: jo maageh thaakur apune te, soee soee devai. Whatever is asked of one's own Master, that very thing He gives.
It continues, in effect: whatever the servant Nanak speaks, it comes true, here and hereafter. Thaakur is master, lord, the one you belong to.

Notice the small word apune, your own: not a distant ruler you petition through officials, but your own Master, the one who already knows you. Now, the honest question. Does this mean a person gets anything they want?

The hymn gives the context. The one speaking is the daas, the servant: Nanak calls himself that in the very next line. One reading is that a servant who lives close to the Master starts to want what the Master wants.
Elsewhere Gurbani speaks of bhaana, the Will, and of asking first for the Name.

teach.h: THE SERVANT WHO ASKS IN TRUST.
teach.b: So the line is less a blank check than a picture of trust between a servant and a good master: the servant isn't afraid to ask, and the Master doesn't hold back.

teach.h: NOT A BLANK CHECK: THE WILL.
teach.b: Some Sikhs also say, from experience, that what's given is sometimes not what was asked, but what was needed: strength instead of escape, patience instead of speed.
Look back at the week. Partners, all. Pitaa.
Kaudi: not for a shell. Hargobind, a gift arriving. One father, all his children.
And now thaakur: a week about belonging, and about asking like someone who belongs.

how: Sikhs sing Guru Arjan's Dhanasri shabad in kirtan and often recall its line 'jo maageh thaakur apune te soee soee devai' when making an Ardas, alongside acceptance of the Will.

o: master, lord, the one you belong to
a servant who asks his master in trust
a ruler reached only through officials

games.q: whatever you ask — tap the pairs.

s: the line is a blank check for anything you want
it pictures a servant's trust; Gurbani also asks for the Name first and accepts the Will.
the line speaks of your own Master, not a distant ruler
apune: your own, the one who already knows you.

games.q: you've read: whatever you ask of your own Master, He gives. what do you ask for?
o: one truly good thing, in trust.
nothing; it's too good to be true.
games.why: the line is spoken by a servant, the daas, who trusts the Master enough to ask plainly.

practice: Let your wants come up, the big and the petty, without judging them, then let them settle and see which one is truly good, for you and for others: courage, maybe, or healing for someone, or patience with a child.
If you pray, you can ask the One for it simply, the way a child asks a parent they trust; if you don't, hold it as a hope.

wordCard.voice: Thaakur, master, lord, the one you belong to: Guru Arjan says whatever is asked of your own thaakur, He gives; the trust of a servant who belongs.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: master, lord; jo maageh thaakur apune te, whatever is asked of one's own Master.

carryVoice: Your line: ask your master. Trust, not a blank check. A week of belonging, complete.
